segments.title: Examples of Big O Notation in Programming

sub_topics.name: Example 1: Add Up Function
sub_topics.description: Here's a more concrete example. I have a function named addup. We will add up to a certain number depending on what we pass in as an argument. The for loop within here will iterate once up to whatever number that n is, add i to sum, then return it. What if n was a large number like a million? Well, it's going to take just above a million steps to complete this function. This function is said to have a runtime complexity of O of n, linear time.

sub_topics.name: Example 2: Constant Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: Now another way which we could write the same function is to take sum equals n times n plus 1 divided by 2. We will get the exact same sum. So if n was, let's say, a million, this is still only going to take a couple seconds. steps. Three steps, not a million steps. So this function is going to have a runtime complexity of O of one. segments.title: Overview of Runtime Complexities in Big O Notation

sub_topics.name: Constant Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: So let begin with O of 1 constant time. Anything that has a runtime complexity of O of 1 will take the same amount of time regardless of the data size. A few examples would include the random access of an element within an array and inserting at the beginning of a linked list.

sub_topics.name: Logarithmic Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: Next we have O of log n, also known as logarithmic time. One example is binary search. We haven't talked about this yet. We'll talk about a few of these algorithms in future videos, but anything that has a runtime complexity of O of log n will actually take, I don't want to say less and less time, but increasingly less time to complete.

sub_topics.name: Linear Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: O is also known as linear time. As the amount of data increases, the time it takes to complete something will increase proportionally linearly. That would include looping through the elements in an array and searching through a linked list.

sub_topics.name: Quasi-Linear Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: Next we have O of N log N, also known as quasi-linear time. This would include a quick sort, merge sort, and heap sort. We'll talk about these concepts in future videos. So for the most part, this is very similar to linear time. Unless we're working with a large data set, then anything using O of N log N is going to start to slow down when we work with larger data sets, hence this curve here.

sub_topics.name: Quadratic Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: Then we have O of n squared, also known as quadratic time. A few examples would include insertion sort, selection sort, and bubble sort. As the amount of data increases, it's going to take increasingly more and more time to complete anything that has a runtime complexity of O of n squared.

sub_topics.name: Factorial Time Complexity
sub_topics.description: And lastly, we have O of n factorial, also known as factorial time, and one place where this is used is with the traveling salesman problem, which I might discuss in a future video.
